methodological_rigor.justification: The retrospective single-center cohort design (n=86; 29 melanomas, 57 nevi) is appropriate for a head-to-head comparison but modest, and no a priori power calculation is reported. The analytic plan is sensible and well-executed: pre-specified one-sided Jonckheere-Terpstra, linear regression, univariable and multivariable logistic regression with Tjur R2, AIC, Hosmer-Lemeshow, DeLong tests, and 2000-resample bootstrap internal validation with optimism correction (apparent AUC 0.93, optimism-corrected 0.92, calibration slope 0.89). Weaknesses include no histopathologic ground truth, author-acknowledged shared-feature incorporation bias between MOLES and the expert reference, imbalanced MOLES categories (46 at score 0 vs 8 at >=4), lack of external validation, and reliance on the low-power Hosmer-Lemeshow test in a small sample. Effect sizes and CIs are consistently reported.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is an individual retrospective cohort evaluating diagnostic/triage performance of two scoring systems against expert multimodal diagnosis, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is plausible but not practice-changing: triage of small pigmented choroidal lesions is a real clinical bottleneck, and a reproducible photo-based AI could help optometrists and non-expert ophthalmologists, but the reference standard is expert diagnosis rather than patient outcomes (metastasis/survival), and MOLES was applied by subspecialists so non-expert generalizability is not tested here. The findings refine understanding of complementary triage tools but do not yet alter guidelines.

reporting_quality.justification: The study is a diagnostic accuracy comparison of two index tests (MOLES and MelAInoma) against an expert reference standard, making STARD the most applicable checklist (TRIPOD is also partly relevant for the multivariable model). Inclusion/exclusion criteria, imaging modalities, scoring procedures, and statistical methods are well described, with ethics approval (reference 2025-05054-01) and software versions (R 4.4.3, GraphPad Prism 10.6.1, MelAInoma v0.1) stated. Key STARD gaps include absence of a patient flow diagram, no protocol registration, limited pre-specification of thresholds or primary analysis, no indeterminate-result handling, and no reported inter-rater reliability for MOLES. No data-availability or code-availability statement is present in the manuscript text, so reproducibility posture is limited to the described methods.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is empirical and incremental: both MOLES (reference 20, 21) and MelAInoma (reference 19) are previously published tools, and the authors have already evaluated them separately in optician triage settings (reference 15). The specific contribution is a direct head-to-head comparison on an independent cohort with multivariable modeling showing partially non-overlapping information (R2 = 0.16; both independently associated after mutual adjustment). This represents a meaningful but modest extension of prior work in one direction rather than a new mechanism, model, or population; the ocular oncology AI space already includes similar photo-based classifiers (e.g., reference 31).

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and logically organized, with a lay-language opening paragraph followed by a structured scientific abstract, well-sign-posted methods, and clearly numbered results subsections mirroring each analysis (JT, linear regression, univariable/multivariable logistic, bootstrap, imaging-modality subgroup). Acronyms (OCT, LBD, AMD, ICD-10) are expanded on first use, and the discussion carefully delineates concordance, discordance, and the shared-feature incorporation concern. The Strengths and Limitations section is thorough (eight numbered limitations). Minor issues: one awkward sentence (section 3.6: 'showed substantially improved the fit'), occasional redundancy between results text and tables, and reliance on figures that cannot be assessed from captions in this blinded version.

key_strengths: Pre-specified, appropriate statistical plan with effect sizes, 95% CIs, Tjur R2, AIC, Hosmer-Lemeshow, DeLong, and 2000-resample bootstrap internal validation (apparent AUC 0.93; optimism-corrected 0.92; calibration slope 0.89)
Independent test cohort not used for MelAInoma training, with >=5-year follow-up requirement for nevus classification strengthening the reference standard
Transparent, candid limitations section explicitly flagging shared-feature incorporation bias favoring MOLES
Direct, clinically motivated head-to-head comparison of a manual (MOLES) and AI (MelAInoma) triage tool with multivariable mutual-adjustment showing complementary information
Clear, well-organized writing with a lay summary, structured abstract, and logically numbered results
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective cohort (n=86) with no a priori power calculation and imbalanced MOLES strata (46 at score 0 vs 8 at >=4), limiting generalizability and category-specific precision
No histopathologic ground truth; reference is expert clinical diagnosis, with acknowledged shared-feature incorporation bias between MOLES and the reference
No external validation; bootstrap addresses optimism but not transportability, and only expert graders applied MOLES, so the intended non-expert use case is not tested here
STARD/TRIPOD gaps: no patient flow diagram, no protocol registration, no pre-specified primary analysis or diagnostic thresholds in this study, no inter-rater reliability for MOLES
No data- or code-availability statement in the manuscript text; MelAInoma is a proprietary commercial product (Eyedentity AB), further limiting reproducibility
Surrogate endpoint (expert diagnosis) rather than patient-relevant outcomes such as metastasis or survival
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competently executed, well-written but incremental single-center diagnostic comparison with modest sample size, no external validation, and acknowledged incorporation bias; it is a credible fit for a mid-tier oncology or ophthalmic-oncology journal (Tier 3) with minor revisions addressing reporting-standard gaps and data/code availability.
